# Tests That Pass for the Wrong Reason

A failing test tells you something is broken. A **passing** test tells you nothing at all unless you
know it could have failed. [[python-programming-laboratories]] documents two concrete instances, both
of which pass against an implementation that does nothing.

## Instance 1 — the assertion never reached the code

> "**An assertion has to reach the code under test.** A test whose argument is an undefined name
> raises `NameError` while evaluating the call, before the function is entered — so
> `pytest.raises(TypeError)` never sees it, and the test would pass against an implementation doing no
> type checking at all."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/labs/07_testing/README.md, 2026-07-25

The mechanics: `pytest.raises(TypeError)` is a context manager, and `NameError` is not `TypeError`
— but the argument expression is evaluated *before* the call, and in this case raised inside the
`raises` block. The test is green, the function was never invoked, and deleting the entire type check
from the implementation changes nothing.

The general failure: **an exception raised while building the call is indistinguishable from one
raised by the call** unless you check which. Assert on the exception's message or type precisely, and
be suspicious of any `raises` block containing more than the single call under test.

## Instance 2 — `"no"` is truthy

Lab 09 generates fixtures with [[factory-boy-and-faker]], and the trap is in the data rather than the
control flow: a CSV field containing the string `"no"` is truthy in Python. A test that populates
every field with plausible values and asserts on a filter can pass because *everything* passed the
filter, not because the filter worked.

The discipline the lab adopts is the fix: **factories fill the irrelevant fields; each test sets the
field under test explicitly.** A fixture that decides the value under test has moved the assertion
into the fixture, where nobody reads it.

## How the labs make the tests capable of failing

- **Validation order is pinned by tests**, not just validation outcome — so a refactor that checks
  arguments in a different sequence fails loudly.
- **`parametrize` across methods and versions**, so a test that only passes for `GET` and `HTTP/1.1`
  is exposed.
- Round-trip properties (parse → format → parse) rather than fixed expected strings — see
  [[common-log-format-parsing]].

## The wider point

This is the reason [[python-programming-laboratories]] lists "knowing when a test passes for the
wrong reason" as a skill rather than "writing tests". A suite's value is its **discriminating power**,
and that is not measured by count. The repo's own "89 tests" headline is exactly the kind of number
this concept warns about — see [[pytest]].
